note: Sources assessed and declined, with what was found. Declining after looking is a result; declining without looking is a gap.

declined.source: Antenati — the nine sitemaps other than ant_archivio
looked: story_location-sitemap.xml — 59 urls, story TAGS (Alfenas, Americana, Bari) marking where a family story is set
ant_storia-sitemap.xml + 2 — 140 family stories and blog posts
post-sitemap, dmc_users_nationality, story_author, story_nationality — editorial taxonomy
declined.why: Antenati's remaining sitemaps carry the portal's magazine — family stories, author pages, the nationality tags on them. Charming, and not a statement about where any record is held. The one sitemap that was archival, ant_archivio, gave all 119 state archives and has been harvested. There is no second file here.

declined.name: IrishGenealogy.ie — bulk harvest of its record locations
declined.verdict: declined by this project, not by the site
declined.why: Behind a Cloudflare MANAGED CHALLENGE. It loads perfectly in a human's browser and answers 403 to everything else, and its own challenge page carries «noindex, nofollow» — that is a site saying plainly that it does not want to be read by a script. Working around a bot gate is not something this project will do, whatever the data is worth. IrishGenealogy stays what it already is here: a provider row with a link a human clicks, and it is the best free national source in these islands. The record-location question it was asked to answer is answered instead by Townlands.ie, which publishes the whole county–barony–civil parish–townland hierarchy as an open download. See scripts/harvest-ireland.py.

declined.name: Matricula Online — bulk harvest of its parish inventory
declined.why: Matricula is one of the best things on this map — free scans of parish registers for Austria, Germany, Poland, Slovenia, Italy and Serbia — and its terms put the images AND THEIR DESCRIPTIVE METADATA under CC BY-NC-ND 2.0. Non-commercial. This site carries advertising, so republishing its parish inventory as part of an ad-supported dataset is exactly what that licence refuses, and the fact that the metadata would be useful is not an argument against the licence. It stays a provider row with a link, which the licence plainly permits and which is what a reader needs anyway. If the ad slot is ever turned off, this is worth asking them about directly.

declined.name: National Archives Catalog (NARA) — API key
declined.why: NARA's catalog API issues keys to a named person via a signup form. Nothing here can complete that, and nothing here should try. Listed so the gap is visible rather than mistaken for an absence of American records.

declined.name: Szukaj w Archiwach — bulk harvest of its fonds list
declined.why: The Polish state archives' own portal, holding the fonds inventory for Poland and much of western Ukraine and Belarus. Behind Incapsula: /api answers with an Incapsula challenge page carrying «NOINDEX, NOFOLLOW». Same judgement as IrishGenealogy — that is a site saying it does not want to be read by a script, and this project will not work around a bot gate. It stays a provider row.

declined.name: Scotland's civil and old parishes, as boundaries or a list
declined.verdict: FOUND — this entry stood for two hours
declined.why: KEPT AS A RECORD OF A PREMATURE GIVE-UP. The first search concluded Scotland's parishes were not openly available: nrscotland.gov.uk's civil-parishes page 404s, statistics.gov.scot did not answer at all, scotlandsplaces.gov.uk is a search box with no download, and the National Library of Scotland's boundary pages are behind a CAPTCHA. Four closed doors read as a closed building. They were not: data.gov.uk lists «Civil Parishes - Scotland», and behind it National Records of Scotland runs a live WFS that hands over the whole layer on request. 871 parishes, OGL v3.0, and 870 of them are now drawn. The lesson is the entry: «not found» is a statement about the search, and this file exists so the next search starts further along rather than repeating this one. See scripts/harvest-scotland-parishes.py.

declined.name: England and Wales registration districts
declined.why: UKBMD publishes the registration-district hierarchy and its sub-districts, which is what the GRO indexes are arranged by, and states no reuse licence. Vision of Britain holds the historic administrative units and has moved everything except the GB1900 gazetteer behind the UK Data Service, which needs a named academic registration. GB1900 itself is CC BY-SA and downloadable, but it is 2.5 million map labels — farms, hills and streams — rather than a list of filing units, so it is the wrong shape for this even though it is the right licence.

declined.name: German Standesamt districts, 1874 onwards
declined.why: Civil registration in Prussia from October 1874 is filed by Standesamt, and there is no open national list of the historical ones — the modern registry offices are a different and much smaller set after a century of amalgamation. The GenWiki community holds the best inventory and its licence is unclear. Recorded so the next attempt starts from here rather than from Destatis.

declined.name: The National Archives, Discovery — the UK repositories directory
declined.verdict: open, and the sweep parameter is wrong
declined.why:
THIS WAS LISTED AS «NEEDS A HUMAN TO REGISTER» AND THAT WAS WRONG. Discovery's API needs no key, no token and no account — David went looking for the key request page on my say-so and there is no such page. Verified anonymously: three endpoints, three 200s.

The harvester is written (scripts/harvest-tna-archives.py) and does not work yet, and the reason turned out not to be the rate limit it was first blamed on. It sweeps by `sps.titleFirstLetter`, which Discovery does not accept — the endpoint answers perfectly to `sps.searchQuery` and returns nothing at all for a parameter it does not know, which is the most expensive kind of silence. An empty answer was read as «blocked», the harvester backed off politely, and the real fault sat untouched for an hour. It needs a different sweep: searchQuery against a vocabulary of terms, or the county and repository-type facets the response already returns.

Worth the wait: Discovery indexes roughly two and a half thousand British repositories with their addresses — the county record offices where English parish registers actually live.

declined.name: Indeks — Hrvatsko rodoslovno društvo, bulk read of its index
declined.why: Its robots.txt is not a generic crawl-delay: it lists twenty-one AI and LLM agents — ClaudeBot, Claude-Web and anthropic-ai among them — disallows each from the whole site, and then explicitly allows everyone else, under the heading «keep them off the index data». That is not a gate that happened to catch us; it is a Croatian genealogical society saying which readers it does not want, and this atlas is one of them. Nothing here was read beyond robots.txt itself. It keeps a provider row, because a link a human clicks is the thing they built it for, and pointing researchers at it costs them nothing they objected to.

declined.name: Acta Croatica — ingesting its surname statistics
declined.verdict: declined on provenance and licence, not on access
declined.why: The pages are open and its robots.txt is empty, so this is a choice rather than a wall. A surname page is genuinely the best thing of its kind — for Horvat it gives 19,900 people in 8,100 households, the five towns holding most of them with counts, the mid-century figure for comparison, fourteen countries emigrated to with counts, and nine spelling variants. But the site states no licence at all, and its prose says «according to some sources» without naming them. This atlas's rule is that every row carries a checked date and a resolvable provider; importing derived counts whose derivation is not stated would put unsourced numbers behind a map that promises the opposite. Note the disagreement it exposes, which is worth more than the rows would have been: Acta Croatica and Wikipedia both give Horvat as about 19,700–19,900, and DZS's own 2011 census lookup answers 21,618. Three sources, one census, three numbers. That is the argument for taking the primary one and saying which it is. Acta Croatica keeps a provider row with a per-surname deep link.

declined.name: Geneanet — its surname pages
declined.why: Answers 403 to a plain request while loading for a human, which is the same wall as IrishGenealogy and Antenati. Not climbed. Geneanet already has a provider row here and keeps it. What is worth taking from it is not its data but its shape — a page per surname showing where the name is thickest and how it is spelled elsewhere — and this atlas can build that from sources that let it: see the per-place surname counts it already holds.

declined.name: Genealogia w Archiwach — harvesting its holdings
declined.verdict: impractical, which is not the same as refused
declined.why: Worth separating from the other entries in this file. Antenati, IrishGenealogy and Geneanet say no: a 403, a managed challenge, a robots.txt naming this agent. This one says nothing at all. It is a Vaadin 7 application, and every url returns the same two-kilobyte shell — /robots.txt and /sitemap.xml included, which is how you can tell there is no crawlable surface rather than a closed one. The holdings move over Vaadin's stateful UIDL protocol, so reading them means driving a session, and a session is not a dataset. Nothing here is being refused and no gate is being honoured; the site simply has no interface to read. If the Polish archives publish a catalogue elsewhere — and Szukaj w Archiwach is the obvious place — that is the route, not this.

declined.source: agatha.arch.be — the State Archives of Belgium's catalogue
looked: arch.be links to it as «Genealogical sources» from Online resources
TLS 1.3 handshake completes and the certificate verifies
the connection is then closed without an HTTP response (curl exit 56)
a real browser was refused the navigation as well
declined.why: This is the LIVE successor to the retired search.arch.be — arch.be's own «Online resources» page links to https://agatha.arch.be/search/genealogie/ as its genealogical search. It answers a TLS handshake and then hangs up without an HTTP response, and refuses a real browser from here too, which is a gate and not an outage. This project does not work around gates or claim to be a browser it is not, so agatha stays out of the provider list until it will talk to an ordinary client or somebody asks its keepers. David raised it directly, so it is written down rather than silently dropped.
